issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly characterizes the data as a national probability/general population/nationally representative sample, but the Methods describe a psychology student participant pool with a young, predominantly female, predominantly Pākehā sample. This contradiction undermines interpretation, external validity, and the framing of the study's contribution.
issues.quote: Abstract: "We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years." ... Introduction: "We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years" ... Method: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington."

issues.description: The sample is a convenience sample of university students, yet the paper claims results generalize to the New Zealand population and discusses implications for 'the general population.' This is a substantial overclaim because age, education, student status, ethnicity, and political socialization likely moderate ideology-environment relations.
issues.quote: "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population."

issues.description: The manuscript alternates among several different outcomes—"willingness to change behaviour," "willingness to sacrifice for the environment," and "concern about environmental problems"—as if they were the same construct. The Methods define environmentalism using concern items, but the analysis and tables label the variable as willingness to sacrifice (WILL). This creates ambiguity about what was actually measured and analyzed.
issues.quote: Abstract: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment"; Methods: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems."; Data Analysis: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment."; Table note: "WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment."

issues.subcategory: measure does not match target construct
issues.description: The environmentalism measure described in Methods consists of two items assessing concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems, but the manuscript interprets findings as willingness to make personal sacrifices/behavior change. Concern is not equivalent to willingness to sacrifice behaviorally; conflating these constructs threatens construct validity and overstates behavioral implications.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'"

issues.subcategory: missing item content for focal outcome
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide the actual items for the purported dependent variable used in the analyses if it is indeed 'willingness to sacrifice'/'willingness to make sacrifices.' Instead, it reports concern items. This prevents evaluation of scale content, scoring, and comparability with prior work.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale..."

issues.description: Environmentalism is operationalized with only two items, and one appears reverse-worded about exaggeration of problems. A two-item measure provides limited coverage of a multidimensional construct and increases measurement error, especially problematic in longitudinal SEM where stable trait-like constructs are modeled across five waves.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems... 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'"

issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics and reliabilities are presented, despite a five-wave longitudinal analysis. Reliability and descriptive information at later waves are necessary to assess temporal stability, possible drift, and whether stationarity assumptions are plausible.
issues.quote: "Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1."

issues.description: Using listwise deletion in a five-wave panel can induce substantial bias and loss of power unless data are missing completely at random. The manuscript does not justify this choice, report amount/pattern of missingness, or test MCAR/MAR assumptions. Full-information maximum likelihood would generally be preferable for SEM with longitudinal missingness.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.description: The manuscript does not report retention rates by wave, dropout patterns, or whether attrition was associated with ideology or environmentalism. Referring readers to an external website is insufficient for evaluating risk of attrition bias in the present analysis.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: The analytic syntax is said to be available only 'upon acceptance,' which prevents proper peer evaluation and reproducibility during review. Key information needed to verify model specification should be included in the manuscript or supplement available to reviewers.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.description: No preregistration or prior analysis plan is reported, despite many plausible researcher degrees of freedom in longitudinal modeling (e.g., stationarity constraints, handling of missing data, equality constraints, residual structure). Without preregistration, the chosen model may reflect post hoc optimization.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant."

issues.description: The authors impose a stationary cross-lagged model with equal parameters across all intervals because they are 'more interested in overall and comparative effects,' but do not test whether these equality constraints are empirically tenable. In a student sample spanning ages ~19 to ~23, developmental changes and varying interval dynamics are plausible; forcing stationarity can mask time-specific effects or distort estimates.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.description: The paper refers to 'five years' and 'five semesters' from 2009 to 2013. Semesters are not the same as annual waves. The exact timing between measurements is unclear, which matters for interpreting cross-lagged coefficients and the stationarity assumption.
issues.quote: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.description: The manuscript describes the study as a five-year analysis, but Methods say participants were surveyed across five semesters from 2009 to 2013. Five semesters over 2009–2013 does not clearly map onto five annual observations, creating uncertainty about the temporal design.
issues.quote: Title: "A five-year cross-lagged analysis" ... Method: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.description: Longitudinal comparisons and cross-lagged paths assume that constructs are measured equivalently across waves. The manuscript does not report any tests of longitudinal measurement invariance for SDO, RWA, or environmentalism. This is especially problematic because one RWA item was missing at Time 2 and short scales can be unstable.
issues.quote: "The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.description: One RWA item was absent at Time 2, meaning the scale differs across waves. Without explicit modeling of this non-equivalence and invariance testing, observed change or lagged relations involving RWA may partly reflect measurement artifacts rather than substantive change.
issues.quote: "The item ... was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.description: The manuscript mentions constraining residual variance for 'the same item over time,' suggesting an item-level latent SEM, but also presents only scale reliabilities and path analysis language. It never clearly states whether constructs were modeled as latent variables, observed composites, or item parcels. This omission prevents evaluation of parameter meaning and model adequacy.
issues.quote: "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.description: The description of model constraints repeats the same sentence about constraining cross-lagged associations, suggesting possible editing error and leaving unclear what additional constraints (e.g., autoregressive paths, residual covariances, intercepts) were imposed.
issues.quote: "We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. ... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point."

issues.description: Regression/path estimates are reported as 'B = ..., SD = ...' where the second quantity appears to be the standard error, not a standard deviation. Using SD instead of SE is statistically incorrect and confusing.
issues.quote: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])."

issues.description: Several chi-square difference/Wald-like tests are reported without the chi-square symbol, e.g., '2(1) = 2.34'. This appears to be a formatting/statistical notation error and obscures the exact test used.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126"

issues.description: The authors conclude SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA despite reporting that constraining the paths equal did not significantly worsen fit (p = .126). A non-significant difference test means the data do not support the claim that the predictive paths differ. Interpreting coefficient magnitudes alone as evidence of a stronger effect is incorrect.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample."

issues.subcategory: claim of significant stronger predictor contradicts reported test
issues.description: The paper repeatedly states that SDO is a significantly stronger predictor than RWA, but the reported equality-constraint comparison is non-significant. This contradiction affects the main conclusion.
issues.quote: Results: "we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor" after p = .126; Discussion: "In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.description: The reported test comparing the lagged effects of RWA→SDO and SDO→RWA is extraordinarily large relative to the tiny coefficients and sample size (χ² = 15,389.13 with 1 df), suggesting a reporting, coding, or model-comparison error.
issues.quote: "These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames cross-lagged associations as establishing causal pathways. Standard cross-lagged panel models with observational data do not identify causation because they remain vulnerable to unmeasured stable and time-varying confounds, measurement error, and model misspecification. At most, the analyses show temporal precedence/association under assumptions.
issues.quote: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism."

issues.description: Even within the authors' own model, environmentalism predicts later ideology. Yet the Discussion privileges ideology as causal and even 'foundational.' Given reciprocal effects and possible omitted confounds, such asymmetrical causal interpretation is not warranted.
issues.quote: "With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes."

issues.description: The authors briefly acknowledge possible third-variable explanations only in the Discussion, but the analyses do not adjust for plausible confounders such as political ideology, socioeconomic status, economic insecurity, education, or party identification. Without these controls, cross-lagged paths may reflect omitted variable bias.
issues.quote: "Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable."

issues.description: No demographic or political covariates are included, despite likely confounding of SDO/RWA and environmentalism by age, gender, ethnicity, SES, political orientation, religiosity, and education. In a student sample with limited variance, some of these may still matter, and omission complicates interpretation of estimated cross-lags.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points"

issues.description: The manuscript states that social dominance theory proposes SDO and RWA are 'separate but interrelated,' but the cited foundational source for social dominance theory concerns SDO; RWA is from a distinct theoretical tradition and dual-process models typically treat them as distinct ideological attitudes with different antecedents. This conflation blurs theoretical frameworks.
issues.quote: "Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups."

issues.description: The abstract and discussion infer specific motivations ('desire for dominance' and 'desire to submit to tradition and authority') from associations between broad scales and environmental attitudes. These mechanistic claims are not directly tested in the study and exceed the evidence.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority."

issues.description: The authors note lower reliabilities for abbreviated SDO and RWA scales but proceed without discussing implications for attenuation, measurement error, or potential bias in cross-lagged estimates. Short scales may underestimate associations and complicate longitudinal modeling.
issues.quote: "Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31]."

issues.description: Cronbach's alpha or other reliability estimate is provided for SDO and RWA in Table 1 but not for the environmentalism/WILL measure, despite it being a focal outcome and apparently based on only two items.
issues.quote: Table 1 shows diagonal reliabilities for SDO (.69) and RWA (.70) and WILL (.76), but the manuscript text only comments on SDO and RWA reliabilities: "Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer..."

issues.description: Table 1 labels the environmental variable 'WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment,' but Methods define environmentalism via concern/exaggeration items. This inconsistency suggests either the wrong table was inserted, the wrong methods description was given, or a different measure was analyzed than described.
issues.quote: Table note: "WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment."

issues.description: The authors accept the model despite poor CFI (.86), justifying this by saying some indices are affected by model complexity. While RMSEA can remain low in large complex models, dismissing poor CFI without sensitivity analyses or alternative models is questionable, especially for a highly constrained longitudinal SEM.
issues.quote: "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03 ...), therefore the model was accepted."

issues.subcategory: figure values not actually available in manuscript text
issues.description: The results depend heavily on Figure 1 for autoregressive and path parameters, but the manuscript excerpt provides no actual figure values. Readers cannot verify all parameters, residual correlations, or the pattern of constraints from the text alone.
issues.quote: "Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL)."

issues.subcategory: standard CLPM may confound between- and within-person effects
issues.description: A traditional cross-lagged panel model is used, but such models conflate stable between-person differences with within-person change. For trait-like constructs such as SDO and RWA, this is especially problematic; a random-intercept CLPM or related model would better isolate within-person dynamics. Without this, cross-lagged paths may primarily reflect stable trait covariance rather than change processes.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant."

issues.description: The manuscript claims the analyses 'help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships.' Standard observational CLPMs do not definitively disentangle directionality because multiple causal structures can produce the same lagged pattern, especially under omitted variables and between-person confounding.
issues.quote: "These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships"

issues.subcategory: no sample size by wave / effective N for model
issues.description: The manuscript states that 374 participants were included but does not report how many contributed data at each wave or the effective sample after listwise deletion. In a five-wave model, the complete-case N could be much smaller than 374.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study..."

issues.description: A five-wave three-construct cross-lagged SEM with item-level indicators and many equality constraints is estimated on a modest sample of 374, potentially much smaller after listwise deletion. This raises concerns about precision, power, convergence, and stability of estimates, especially for small cross-lagged effects like RWA→environmentalism.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study... The model included three variables across five measurement points"

issues.subcategory: lack of estimator and treatment of ordinal items
issues.description: The manuscript does not report the Mplus estimator (e.g., ML, MLR, WLSMV) or whether the 7-point Likert items were treated as continuous or ordinal. This affects standard errors, fit indices, and interpretation of coefficients.
issues.quote: "The model ... was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29])."

issues.subcategory: missing details of confidence interval computation
issues.description: Table 1 says CIs are based on '1000 iterations' but does not explain whether these are bootstrap confidence intervals, Monte Carlo intervals, or something else. The same ambiguity applies to whether model-based CIs for paths were bootstrapped or asymptotic.
issues.quote: "Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations."

issues.description: The Methods state a significance threshold of p < .05, while Figure 1 is described as using p < .01 as the accepted threshold. This inconsistency creates ambiguity about inferential criteria.
issues.quote: Methods: "we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05"; Figure caption: "All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted."

issues.subcategory: misuse of large-sample rationale for alpha level
issues.description: The authors justify p < .05 by citing the large sample size, but larger samples typically increase power and can make trivial effects statistically significant; this does not justify a conventional alpha, nor address practical significance. The rationale is conceptually backwards.
issues.quote: "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings."

issues.description: The paper recommends targeting high-SDO individuals with climate-change communications and suggests framing strategies, but the study does not test interventions, message framing, or behavior change. Translational claims exceed observational attitudinal evidence.
issues.quote: "Our findings highlight endorsers of SDO as targets for climate change communications. One possible next step is to explore the effects of framing climate change messages in ways that could motivate high-SDO individuals to act."

issues.description: The authors infer from asymmetric cross-lags that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This is a strong sociocultural claim not directly measured and not warranted from a student panel from one university.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."

issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly young, female, and Pākehā, but limitations do not adequately discuss how these demographics constrain transferability of ideology-environment links to older, male, Māori, Pasifika, or more socioeconomically diverse populations.
issues.quote: "the average age was 19 years at Time 1 ... and 68% were female ... the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā"

issues.description: While blinding is less central in survey work, the manuscript provides no information on attention checks, response quality screening, duplicate participation safeguards, or administration conditions, limiting evaluation of data quality.
issues.quote: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington."

issues.subcategory: reference to NZAVS inconsistent with actual recruitment source
issues.description: The manuscript thanks the NZAVS team and directs readers to the NZAVS website for sample details, implying use of NZAVS data, yet the Methods describe recruitment through a university participant pool. This creates confusion about the data source itself.
issues.quote: Methods: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." ... Acknowledgments: "We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team for their work collecting and maintaining the NZAVS."
